content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new method for universal domain adaptation without the source data. This method mainly exploits the entropy-based separation like DANCE [Saito et al. NeurIPS 2021] but utilizes a confidence-guided entropy score. Such a score combines the confidence score and the entropy score in a multiplication manner. Besides, a likelihood-induced energy objective is introduced to minimize the energy of known samples and maximize the energy of unknown samples. Results on several datasets including Office, Office-Home, and DomainNet show that the proposed method outperforms previous methods like UMAD [Liang et al. arxiv 2021] in terms of the H-score.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros

[1]. since most source-free domain adaptation focus on the closed-set problem setting, the studied problem here is more challenging

[2]. the proposed method is simple and the main idea behind is also easy to follow 

[3]. the empirical results look promising when compared with previous source-free methods and even data-dependent UDA methods 

Cons

[1]. Strictly speaking, universal domain adaptation may indicate the setting studied in DANCE where the proposed method should tackle different UDA scenarios without any prior. However, in this paper, only the open-partial-set domain adaptation scenario is considered. Results on closed-set and partial-set scenarios are welcome if the authors really mean the universality of a domain adaptation method.

[2]. Besides, even under the open-partial-set setting, when the overlap is small or large (changing the target label space), how does the proposed method behave when compared with other UniDA methods?

[3] As for the proposed method, entropy separation is a widely used technique in this field, only incorporating confidence into the entropy is somewhat incremental. The following energy optimization item also heavily relies on the separation, which has already been introduced in several previous works like [a,b]. 

[a]. Xie, Binhui, et al. "Active learning for domain adaptation: An energy-based approach." Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence. Vol. 36. No. 8. 2022.

[b]. Liu, Xiaofeng, et al. "Energy-constrained self-training for unsupervised domain adaptation." 2020 25th International Conference on Pattern Recognition (ICPR). IEEE, 2021.

By the way, Eq.(3) could be simplified as (1-c)log(1-c) + (1-c)H(y). Then more ablation studies could be conducted to verify the contribution of both terms.

content.title: Response (3/3) to Reviewer f4Hb
content.comment:
**4. Hyperparameter $\alpha$.** 

The sensitivity analysis of the hyperparameter $\alpha$ on three tasks from three different datasets is provided in Fig. 5 (Appendix).
Similar to [1, 3, 7], the hyperparameter $\alpha$ in our method is empirically selected by the performance of the A$\rightarrow$D task on the Office-31 dataset, Ar$\rightarrow$Cl task on the Office-Home dataset and train$\rightarrow$val task on the VisDA dataset.
According to the results reported in Fig. 5 (Appendix), $\alpha$ is set as 0.6 for all the experiments.
In our future work, we will design an automatic selection mechanism for this hyperparameter.

**5. Ablation study of the simplified confidence-guided entropy.**

It is correct that the confidence-guided entropy $H_c$ in eq. (3) (Manuscript) can be simplified as $H_c(\hat{y}) = (1 - c)\log (1 - c) + (1 - c)H(\hat{y})$.
The comparison results of $(1 - c)H(\hat{y})$ and $H_c(\hat{y})$ on Office-31 (A$\rightarrow$D), Office-Home (Ar$\rightarrow$Cl) and VisDA datasets for target data separation are provided in Fig. 8 (Appendix).
The results (Fig 8 in Appendix) validate the effectiveness of the proposed confidence-guided entropy for better target data separation.

[2] Liang, Jian, Dapeng Hu, and Jiashi Feng. "Do we really need to access the source data? source hypothesis transfer for unsupervised domain adaptation." ICML, 2020.

content.title: Response (2/3) to Reviewer f4Hb
content.comment:
**3. Novelty of the proposed method compared with existing works.** 

**1) Entropy vs. Confidence-guided Entropy.**
We agree that entropy [1] is widely used in domain adaptation.
However, there are two limitations when using the traditional entropy $H$ for source-free UniDA, i.e., 1) the **inconsistent issue** with the known-class confidence $c$, and 2) the **conservative prediction issue** of known classes.
To overcome these two limitations, we propose a novel metric namely confidence-guided entropy $H_c$.
This novel metric $H_c$ shows **consistency** with the known-class confidence $c$ (Proposition 2 in Manuscript) and gives **less conservative prediction** of known classes (Fig. 1 and Fig. 3 in Manuscript).
We use the proposed $H_c$ to separate the known- and unknown-class samples and define a new loss function. 
With better properties of consistency and less conservative prediction, more discriminative models are learned. 
Despite the simplicity, we would like to argue that the proposed confidence-guided entropy is theoretically different from the traditional entropy.
Thorough analysis (Proposition 2, Fig 1 and Fig 3 in Manuscript) and experimental results (Table 4 in Manuscript and Fig. 8 in Appendix) demonstrate the **effectiveness** of the proposed $H_c$.

**2) Different usage of free energy compared with existing works.**
In [5, 6], free energy is used as a regularization term following the traditional Energy-Based Models. Both of these two methods are developed under the setting of **closed-set** “*non-source-free*” domain adaptation, i.e., *source-domain data is available* **without category shift**.
They **CANNOT** be directly employed in the more challenging source-free UniDA problem.
To address this issue, we derive a new loss function by minimizing the free energy of the target-known data and maximizing that of the unknown one (eq. (10) in Manuscript).
Ablation results in Table 4 (Manuscript) validate that this new loss function helps to improve the performance for source-free UniDA.
Moreover, we compare the proposed E$^2$ method with the ablation of free energy as a regularization term (denoted as E$^2_R$) similar to [5, 6] (i.e., free energy is minimized for all the target data including both known and unknown classes). 
Results are presented in Table 3 (Rebuttal) and Table 4 (Rebuttal). 
From these results in Table 3 (Rebuttal) and Table 4 (Rebuttal), we can see that directly using free energy as a regularization term similar to [5, 6] will degrade the performance in source-free UniDA.
Discussion with these two related works [5, 6] is added to the manuscript (Sec. 2 Related Work).

**Table 3: Results on Office-31 (A$\rightarrow$D) dataset under source-free universal domain adaptation.** 
|                                  |    |    |    | | 
|----------------------------------| --- |---- | --- | --- |
| Method                           | OS | OS$^*$ | UNK | HScore | 
| E$^2_R$  | 89.4 | 90.6 | 77.7 | 83.7 |
| E$^2$ (Ours)                     | 91.6 | 92.6 | 81.7 | 86.8 |

**Table 4: Results on VisDA dataset under source-free universal domain adaptation.** 
|                                  |      |    |       | | 
|----------------------------------|------|---- |-------| --- |
| Method                           | OS   | OS$^*$ | UNK   | HScore | 
| E$^2_R$ | 55.8 | 55.9 | 43.8 | 49.1 |
| E$^2$ (Ours)                     | 60.7 | 59.4 | 67.8  |63.4 |

**3) In-depth theoretical analysis based on thermodynamic system.**
More importantly, we would like to highlight that **one of the major contributions** of the proposed method is **the in-depth theoretical integration of entropy with free energy, which is NOT an incremental work simply combining two less irrelevant modules.** 
The relation between entropy and free energy is **closely related in thermodynamic system**.
Free energy quantifies the capacity of a thermodynamic system to do work, while entropy can be considered as the energy in a thermodynamic system that cannot do work.
The physics interpretation of the proposed method is detailed in Sec. 3.3 (Manuscript). 
**With the insight analysis in physics**, the proposed overall loss function eq. (12) (Manuscript) is equal to the internal energy. 
It is worth noting that internal energy is the total energy of a thermodynamic system **different** from free energy.
Entropy and free energy can be considered as a **disintegration** of internal energy.
Consequently, the proposed method is equivalent to **the optimization of internal energy in thermodynamic system.**

content.title: Response to Reviewer 6Gr7
content.comment:
Thanks for your thoughtful comments.

**1. Contributions of the proposed method.**

The theoretical contributions of the proposed method are two-fold.
The first contribution is to address the two limitations when using the traditional entropy $H$ for source-free UniDA, i.e., 1) the **inconsistent issue** with the known-class confidence $c$, and 2) the **conservative prediction issue** of known classes. 
For this purpose, we propose a novel metric namely confidence-guided entropy $H_c$.
This novel metric $H_c$ shows **consistency** with the known-class confidence $c$ (Proposition 2 in Manuscript) and gives **less conservative prediction** of known classes (Fig. 1 and Fig. 3 in Manuscript).
We use the proposed $H_c$ to separate the known- and unknown-class samples and define a new loss function.
With the better properties of consistency and less conservative prediction, more discriminative models are learned.
Though the proposed confidence-guided entropy $H_c$ is **simple** by scaling the normalized prediction score with the confidence score $c$, the analysis (Proposition 2, Fig 1 and Fig 3 in Manuscript) and experimental results (Table 4 in Manuscript and Fig. 8 in Appendix) demonstrate the **effectiveness** of $H_c$.

The second contribution of the proposed method is **the in-depth theoretical integration of entropy with free energy, which is NOT an incremental work simply combining two less irrelevant modules.** 
The relation between entropy and free energy is **closely related in thermodynamic system**.
Free energy quantifies the capacity of a thermodynamic system to do work, while entropy can be considered as the energy in a thermodynamic system that cannot do work.
The physics interpretation of the proposed method is detailed in Sec. 3.3 (Manuscript). 
**With the insight analysis in physics**, the proposed overall loss function eq. (12) (Manuscript) is equal to the internal energy. 
It is worth noting that internal energy is the total energy of a thermodynamic system **different** from free energy.
Entropy and free energy can be considered as the **decomposition** of internal energy.
Consequently, the proposed method is equivalent to **the optimization of internal energy in thermodynamic system.**
Ablation results in Table 4 (Manuscript) validate that the second contribution helps to further improve the
performance for source-free UniDA.

**2. Comparison with the state-of-the-art methods.**

We would like to emphasize that it is **NOT fair** to directly compare the proposed source-free UniDA method E$^2$ with existing “*non-source-free*” methods.
The source-free approach needs not to access the source-domain data for training a target model, while the “*non-source-free*” approach relies on source-domain data for model adaptation.
In our opinion, domain adaptation **without** source data for distribution alignment would limit the **generalization ability** of the model.
As a result, the comparison between the source-free and existing 
“*non-source-free*” UniDA method E$^2$ methods may not be fair.

From Tables 1-3 (Manuscript), we can see that the average HScore performance of the proposed method **outperforms ALL the state-of-the-art source-free domain adaptation** methods.
Moreover, the average HScores of our method are even higher than those of the state-of-the-art “*non-source-free*” UniDA methods on Office-31, Office-Home and VisDA datasets.
Comparing the OS on the Office-31 and the HScore on the DomainNet dataset, our method achieves competitive performance.
All these results convince the effectiveness of the proposed method.

content.title: Response to reviewer WpbQ
content.comment:
Thanks for your precious comments.

**1. Recall under different thresholds.**

In Fig. 1 (Manuscript), the default threshold is set as 0.6 multiplying the maximum of the confidence-guided entropy, i.e., $0.6\log 20=1.8$ for Office-31 (W$\rightarrow$A).
Based on your suggestion, we calculate the recall of the entropy $H$ and the confidence-guided entropy $H_c$ under different thresholds on Office-31 (W$\rightarrow$A) as shown in Table 1 (Rebuttal).
From these results, we can see that the recalls of the proposed $H_c$ are much higher than those of the traditional entropy $H$ under different thresholds. 

**Table 1: Recall of $H$ and $H_c$ under different thresholds on Office-31 (W$\rightarrow$A).**
|           |      |       |
|-----------|------|-------|
| Threshold | $H$  | $H_c$ |
| 1.5       | 0.40 | 0.79  |
| 1.8       | 0.53 | 0.88  |
| 2.0       | 0.63 | 0.92  |

**2. Hyperparamters $\alpha$ and $c$.**

We would like to clarify that the known-class confidence $c$ is **not** a hyperparameter.
It is defined as the maximum of the normalized prediction score, i.e., $c = \max_{i}\hat{y}_i$.
Similar to [1, 2, 3], the hyperparameter $\alpha$ in our method is empirically selected by the performance of the A$\rightarrow$D task on the Office-31 dataset, Ar$\rightarrow$Cl task on the Office-Home dataset and train$\rightarrow$val task on the VisDA dataset.
According to the results reported in Fig. 5 (Appendix), $\alpha$ is set as 0.6 for all the experiments.
In our future work, we will design an automatic selection mechanism for this hyperparameter.

**3. More rigorous results instead of examples.** 

The examples in Lines 7-13 of Sec. 3.1 (Manuscript) illustrate the possible **inconsistency** between the traditional entropy $H$ and the known-class confidence $c$.
Theoretical results about the **consistency** between the known-class confidence $c$ and the proposed confidence-guided entropy $H_c$ are given in Proposition 2 (Manuscript).

**4. Contributions of the proposed method.**

It is true that entropy has been widely used in many existing works about domain adaptation.
However, there are two limitations when using the traditional entropy $H$ for source-free UniDA, i.e., 1) the **inconsistent issue** with the known-class confidence $c$, and 2) the **conservative prediction issue** of known classes.
To overcome these two limitations, we propose a novel metric namely confidence-guided entropy $H_c$.
This novel metric $H_c$ shows **consistency** with the known-class confidence $c$ (Proposition 2 in Manuscript) and gives **less conservative prediction** of known classes (Fig. 1 and Fig. 3 in Manuscript).
We use the proposed $H_c$ to separate the known- and unknown-class samples and define a new loss function.
With better properties of consistency and less conservative prediction, more discriminative models are learned.
This is the first contribution of this work.

The second contribution of our work is  **the in-depth theoretical integration of entropy with free energy, which is NOT an incremental work simply combining two less irrelevant modules.**
The relation between entropy and free energy is **closely related to thermodynamic system**. 
Free energy quantifies the capacity of a thermodynamic system to do work, while entropy can be considered as the energy in a thermodynamic system that cannot do work.
The physics interpretation of the proposed method is detailed in Sec. 3.3 (Manuscript).
**With the insight analysis in physics**, the proposed overall loss function eq. (12) (Manuscript) is equal to the internal energy.
It is worth noting that internal energy is the total energy of a thermodynamic system **different** from free energy.
Entropy and free energy can be considered as the **decomposition** of internal energy.
Consequently, the proposed method is equivalent to **optimization of internal energy in thermodynamic system**.
Ablation results in Table 4 (Manuscript) validate that these two contributions help to improve the performance for source-free UniDA.

**References:**

[1] Saito, Kuniaki, et al. "Universal domain adaptation through self supervision." NeurIPS. 2020.

[2] Saito, Kuniaki, and Kate Saenko. "Ovanet: One-vs-all network for universal domain adaptation." ICCV. 2021.

[3] Li, Guangrui, et al. "Domain consensus clustering for universal domain adaptation." CVPR. 2021.
